item.title: On Keeping a Commonplace Book
item.dc:creator: Ibn Muqla
item.description: A short teaser about commonplace books.
item.content:encoded:
A commonplace book is a reader's memory, written down in the reader's own hand. It is not a diary and it is not a notebook of plans: it is where the passages that stopped you go, so that you can find them again when you need them, and so that they can find each other when you do not.

The oldest ones we have are arranged by heading — Of Friendship, Of Time, Of the Soul — and a passage copied under one heading is a claim about what it means. That claim is the reader's contribution. The passage belongs to somebody else; the heading is yours.

Keep the book near the chair you read in. Copy by hand when you can: the hand is slower than the eye, and the slowness is where the passage goes in. Mark where it came from — the page, the edition — because a passage without a source is a rumour.

Read it back. A commonplace book that is only ever written in is a filing cabinet; one that is read is a conversation between everything you have read, arranged by what you thought it was about at the time you read it.
